plan.summary: A deliberately thin plan: only the two affluent mid-life womenswear publishers (Marlowe & Co., Linden Park) get test budget as the wardrobe-completion hypothesis worth measuring, and everything else is excluded because a $1,200 six-week custom commission is 8-40x every other basket in the catalog with no purchase-level link.

test.name: Marlowe & Co.

signals.name: audience
signals.detail: 96% female; high income for luxury price

test.rationale: A shopper who just bought workwear here is plausibly shopping the same wardrobe a handbag completes, and the notes say this audience "Responds to quality messaging" — the craftsmanship/Florence story is exactly that pitch to an affluent 45-65 female base.
test.risk: $1,200 is roughly 11x the $112 typical basket and the brand ships in 6 weeks with a custom-fit process — a hard ask at a confirmation page where the notes already flag "Lower impulse".

signals.name: audience

test.risk: Still a ~9x price jump, and a conservative 50-70 buyer may balk at a custom-fit configurator plus a 6-week wait; reach is the smallest of the two apparel tests at 6.2M.

bid_strategy.rationale: $1,200 first order × 0.30 = $360.00 target CPA: one-time purchase, so the first order has to pay back the acquisition. The max CPA allows headroom while the campaign learns over 14 days.

test_plan.hypothesis: A shopper who just bought workwear here is plausibly shopping the same wardrobe a handbag completes, and the notes say this audience "Responds to quality messaging" — the craftsmanship/Florence story is exactly that pitch to an affluent 45-65 female base.
test_plan.risk: $1,200 is roughly 11x the $112 typical basket and the brand ships in 6 weeks with a custom-fit process — a hard ask at a confirmation page where the notes already flag "Lower impulse".
test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $360.00 target after 14 days: move it to core.
test_plan.cut_if: CPA above the $468.00 maximum, or no conversions after 14 days: stop it.

test_plan.hypothesis: Classic workwear for affluent 50-70 women is the wardrobe a heritage leather handbag finishes, and at $128 this is the highest-AOV apparel basket available, so the price leap is as small as it gets here.
test_plan.risk: Still a ~9x price jump, and a conservative 50-70 buyer may balk at a custom-fit configurator plus a 6-week wait; reach is the smallest of the two apparel tests at 6.2M.
test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $360.00 target after 14 days: move it to core.
test_plan.cut_if: CPA above the $468.00 maximum, or no conversions after 14 days: stop it.

frequency_cap.rationale: Offers appear once, right after checkout; repeating them reads as spam.

experiment.graduate_rule: After 14 days, move a test publisher to core if its CPA is at or below target; cut any placement above max CPA.
experiment.notes: Creatives rotate evenly until each has enough conversions to compare.

assumptions: Assumed mainly women buyers, typical for handbags.

warnings: The ads for The Gifter, The Sustainability Buyer won't run: no placement's shoppers fit those personas.
No publisher cleared the recommended bar, so the whole budget is a test. Treat results as exploratory.

launch_summary.summary: The full $10,000 is split evenly between Marlowe & Co. and Linden Park, two womenswear publishers whose affluent 45-70 female buyers are the closest match to a wardrobe a Florentine handbag completes. Both run as tests: the question is whether a shopper who just spent around $112-$128 will commit to a $1,200 custom commission with a six-week wait. Target cost per new customer is $360.00, with $468.00 as the ceiling; after 14 days each placement is promoted or cut against those numbers. Expected total is about 28 conversions.
uncertainties: No publisher cleared the recommended fit bar, so all $10,000 is exploratory and the results should be read as a read on the hypothesis, not as performance.
The $360.00 target is 30% of the stated $1,200 first order and assumes a one-time purchase with no repeat value, so real margin or lifetime value would move it.
Only The Affluent Classic ad will run; the Gifter and Sustainability Buyer ads have no matching audience, so the gifting and traceability angles go untested.
questions: What is your actual margin on a $1,200 bag, and do customers ever order again?
Do a meaningful share of these bags get bought as gifts rather than for the buyer?
Is the 30-60 age range right, given both test publishers skew older?
